newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says balanced budget deal first priority.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says balanced budget deal first priority.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he was going to make balancing the federal budget his top priority once a U.S.-Russian summit is over, and hoped to strike a budget deal with Congress this year.

But congressional Republicans said there were still "big differences" on budget issues between them and the Democratic president after Capitol Hill budget committee leaders met Clinton at the White House.
Neither side reported any breakthroughs from the meeting, which the Republicans said was "candid" but a more upbeat Clinton, who had proposed the get-together, labeled it "very productive.

The president said the meeting had given impetus to balancing the budget by the year 2002, an idea which has been languishing in partisan rancour after having been proclaimed earlier this year by all sides as an important goal.

Both sides said they had agreed to meet again over the next two weeks and try to hash out their disagreements on issues ranging from tax cuts to how to gauge inflation and how to rein in the growth of government medical programmes for the elderly and poor.

"Our first order of business when I get back from Helsinki must be to finish the job of balancing the budget. We have to do it this year," Clinton told reporters after the meeting, which a number of senior White House officials also attended.

Clinton said the meetings between some of his staff and the budget committees in the next two weeks should lay the groundwork for a get-together for him with the leadership of the House and Senate and "we will be able to make rapid progress" toward balancing the budget.
"We have circled these issues long enough," the president said. "It's time now to give the American people a balanced budget and I believe we will do it and do it this year."
Clinton was scheduled to leave later Wednesday for Helsinki and return to the White House early Saturday.
House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich said the meeting with Clinton could not be described as either good or bad, but as a "very candid" session.
But he predicted there would be no government shutdown, as there was last year, if Capitol Hill Republicans and Clinton fail to agree on a federal spending plan.
If no agreement is reached, Congress could allow agencies to continue operating at the same spending levels, Kasich, an Ohio Republican, told reporters outside the White House.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, said Republicans would work seriously to narrow the gap on budget ideas, including during the upcoming congressional recess.
"We agreed to work ... to narrow our differences. It is very clear there are big differences," Domenici said.

Almost everyone in Washington voices support for balancing the budget, but there has been little progress toward the goal. Clinton saw a chance for movement this week when House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, suddenly suggested shelving big tax cuts that Democrats opposed.

Gingrich's comment sparked howls of protest from conservatives devoted to cutting taxes. But the Republicans at the budget parley with Clinton did not try to take back what Gingrich had said, one administration official said.

Perhaps the most telling remark about the tone of the session came from New Jersey Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a Democrat, who, when asked whether the Republicans had explained their thinking on tax cuts, replied: "No one was willing to throw out the first card on the table."
The Senate's leading Republican, Trent Lott of Mississippi, suggested the White House engaged in public relations "show and tell" while forgoing chances for a deal.

Lott said he felt Clinton missed a big opportunity to balance the budget by reducing the consumer price index, which is used to calculate the cost of living and thus many federal benefit programmes such as Social Security for retirees. Lott endorsed a commission on the issue, but Clinton did not.
